summary:
Rwanda does not criminalise same-sex intimacy, and the age of consent is 18 regardless of sexual orientation or gender. No statute targets transgender identity or consensual relationships as such.

Rwandan law forbids changing legal gender, so no legal gender recognition path exists. A trans visitor's identity documents cannot be aligned with their lived gender under local law, and identity checks are the point at which that absence becomes an enforcement encounter.

The Human Rights First Rwanda Association's 2025 submission to the UN Human Rights Committee documents law-enforcement abuse directed at transgender people: harassment during identity checks and arbitrary arrests on vagrancy and public-order grounds. Vice reported in November 2020 on violent detentions of transgender people; on Christmas Day 2018 a singer booked to perform at a hotel in Kigali was stopped by police officers on the street after her show, and her name was changed in the reporting because of concerns for her safety. A U.S. State Department report from 2016 recorded LGBTQ Rwandans being harassed, blackmailed and arrested by police under public-order and morality laws, with occasional harassment by neighbours as well as by police.

The Constitution adopted in May 2003 recognises in Article 26 only civil monogamous marriage between a man and a woman. Same-sex marriages, civil unions and comparable unions are not recognised. A trans visitor in a relationship that local law would read as same-sex under birth-sex status has no route to recognition.

No anti-discrimination law covers sexual orientation or gender identity. The Constitution's non-discrimination provisions, Articles 15 and 16, do not list those grounds; Article 16 names ethnic origin, sex, religion, disability and other grounds, but not sexual orientation or gender identity.

The Ministry of Health's Patients Rights and Responsibilities Policy (2018) states that all Rwandans, regardless of gender, sexual orientation, age, religion, cultural belief or disability, are equally entitled to receive health services, and applies across public, private and NGO sectors.

Immigration and asylum protections covering LGBTQ people were issued in 2024, and in April 2022 a transgender claimant was granted refugee status. The Asylum and humanitarian protection decision making Standard Operating Procedures (2024) require interviews to be conducted so that the applicant can present the grounds of their application comprehensively, with trained interviewers taking account of gender and of any circumstance including sexual orientation, gender identity or vulnerability. The Manual on Refugee Appeal Tribunal Standard Operating Procedures (2014) imposes the same requirement on hearings. Standard Operating Procedures on identifying and safeguarding vulnerable persons under the Migration and Economic Development Partnership (2024) define Vulnerable Persons to include individuals whose gender identity or sexual orientation places them at higher risk, expressly naming lesbian, gay, bisexual and transgender persons.

Homosexuality is a taboo subject in Rwanda with no significant public discussion, and LGBTQ people face stigmatisation among the broader population. Asked about LGBT life in Rwanda at Rwanda Cultural Day in San Francisco in September 2016, President Paul Kagame said "it hasn't been our problem. And we don't intend to make it our problem."
tangentialFactors:
Pre-colonial history in the region runs against the current taboo. Anthropologists reported same-sex relations among young Tutsi and Hutu men before colonisation, private and secret. In the old Kingdom of Rwanda, boys training as warriors and Tutsi boys training at court formed emotional and often sexual relationships, sometimes lasting into adulthood, and were sometimes made sexually available to guests. Societal acceptance disappeared after the arrival of European colonialists and Christianity. The historical literature situates Rwanda alongside Uganda and Burundi, which became independent in 1962, and against the memory of the 1994 genocide.

Public visibility has been rare and contested. In September 2019 the gospel singer Albert Nabonibo came out as gay on a Christian YouTube channel, causing shock in a country where such a public assertion is described as unheard of, with hostile reactions from family and friends; the Minister of State for East African Community Affairs, Olivier Nduhungirehe, publicly backed him. The Anglican Church of Rwanda condemned what it called non-biblical behaviours of Western churches in 2007 and refused to support the ordination of LGBTQ clergy.
localsOnly:
No legal gender recognition procedure exists: Rwandan law forbids changing legal gender, so transgender residents hold documents recording the sex assigned at birth.

LGBTIQ organisations cannot register openly, and NGO Law No. 058/2024, adopted in June 2024, raises freedom-of-association concerns. A public Pride event was held in 2021. The Horizons Community Association of Rwanda has conducted public advocacy for LGBTQ rights since 2005, and its members have often been harassed by the government.

Protections that do exist are narrow and sectoral. The Human Resource Management Policy (2015) of the Office of the Auditor General of State Finances lists sexual orientation as a prohibited ground for harassment. The Code of Conduct of the Public Private Partnership Guidelines (2018) bans discrimination against bidders on grounds of sexual orientation. Law 058/2021 on Protection of Personal Data and Privacy protects a person's sexual life as sensitive personal data.
outOfScopeNotes:
No youth-, minor- or education-specific findings appear in the sources: school policy, bullying and the carriage of medication by minors are not documented here.

The asylum and immigration protections are documented as written procedures. Beyond the April 2022 grant of refugee status to a transgender claimant, the sources do not record how those procedures operate in practice.

The most detailed accounts of enforcement against transgender people date from 2016 and 2020; the 2025 submission to the UN Human Rights Committee is the most recent documentation in the inventory. No later presidential statement on the subject appears in the sources, and no reform of the prohibition on changing legal gender is recorded.
